name: Command of Evidence (mixed) 3
description: EBRW FULL · 2 modules × 27 = 54, all original and extremely challenging (literature, science, and historical topics) — same structure and difficulty as English Final 5. Per module: 5 Words in Context + 3 Central Ideas & Details + 7 Command of Evidence + 7 Standard English Conventions + 3 Transitions + 2 Rhetorical Synthesis. Vocabulary from the 550-word SAT list.

questions.passage: Beneath a forest floor lies a vast network of fungal threads that link the roots of different trees. Through this network, trees exchange not only water and nutrients but also chemical signals: a tree under attack by insects can, it seems, warn its neighbors, which then ready their own defenses. The forest, long pictured as a mere collection of individuals competing for light, begins to look instead like a single cooperative organism—though whether the fungi act out of anything resembling altruism, or simply pursue their own advantage, remains fiercely debated.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Trees compete so fiercely for light that they almost never cooperate with one another.
Fungi have been shown to act altruistically to protect the trees whose roots they connect.
Fungal networks beneath a forest floor allow trees to share resources and signals, complicating the view of a forest as merely a set of competing individuals.
Insects pose the single greatest threat to the survival of forest trees.

questions.passage: Popular history likes a lone genius, and so it credits the incandescent light bulb to a single inventor working in a single laboratory. The reality is untidier. Dozens of researchers on three continents had produced glowing filaments before that celebrated "invention"; what the famous inventor and his well-financed team actually achieved was not the first bulb but the first one durable and cheap enough to sell. The myth mistakes the last leg of a long relay for the whole race.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The incandescent light bulb was invented by a single genius working entirely alone.
The inventor usually credited with the light bulb in fact contributed nothing to its development.
Researchers on three continents deliberately concealed their early work on the light bulb.
The famous inventor's real achievement was making an existing invention practical to sell, not inventing the bulb from nothing.

questions.passage: The house was smaller than she remembered—not diminished by neglect, for it had been kept immaculately, but shrunk by the simple fact of her having grown. The great staircase she had once needed both hands to climb she now took in a few unhurried strides; the portraits that had loomed over her childhood met her, at last, at eye level. Nothing had changed, and so everything had.
questions.question: Which choice best describes Eleanor's experience of returning to the house?
options: The house seems altered to her because it has fallen into disrepair during her long absence.
The house seems smaller not because it has changed but because she herself has grown and changed.
She is disappointed to discover that the house has been renovated almost beyond recognition.
She finds that she feels no connection at all to the house she left behind as a child.

questions.passage: The neuroscientist Priya Anand hypothesized that sleep strengthens newly formed memories by "replaying" them: during deep sleep, she proposed, the brain reactivates the same neural patterns that were active during learning, reinforcing them.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Anand's hypothesis?
options: The patterns of brain activity recorded while rats learned a maze reappeared, in compressed form, during the rats' later periods of deep sleep.
Rats deprived of food performed worse on the maze than well-fed rats did.
Humans who sleep more hours per night report feeling more rested than those who sleep fewer.
The maze-learning task activated many different regions of the rats' brains at once.

questions.passage: A company found that employees who drank coffee in the morning completed more tasks over the course of the day than employees who did not, and concluded that drinking coffee boosts productivity.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the company's conclusion?
options: The most driven and ambitious employees were also the ones most likely to drink coffee in the morning, independent of any effect the coffee had.
Employees who completed more tasks also reported enjoying their work more.
Coffee is consumed in most offices around the world.
A few employees drank tea rather than coffee in the morning.

questions.passage: An archaeologist argued that a set of nearly identical stone tools found at sites hundreds of miles apart shows that the tools were traded across long distances rather than invented independently at each site.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the archaeologist's argument?
options: The stone from which all of the tools were made can be traced to a single quarry located near only one of the sites.
Tools of roughly similar shape have also been found on other continents.
The various sites were all occupied during roughly the same period.
Each site also contained tools of several other, quite different shapes.

questions.passage: In an essay, a critic argues that a certain playwright's comedies, for all their surface laughter, are fundamentally pessimistic about human nature.
questions.question: Which quotation from the plays would best support the critic's argument?
options: In the final scene, the schemers are forgiven, the lovers are united, and the household is restored to a happier order than it had ever known.
The playwright's wit is quick, and his verse is among the most musical of the age.
The comedies were performed to great acclaim and filled the city's theaters for decades.
The audience laughs, but the laughter dies in the throat: every character, given the chance to do right, chooses instead the small, mean advantage.

questions.passage: A physiologist proposed that humans can run long distances better than most mammals because we cool ourselves by sweating rather than by panting—an adaptation that frees our breathing from the rhythm of our stride.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the physiologist's proposal?
options: Mammals that cool themselves by panting must synchronize their breathing with their gait, and they tire quickly when forced to run at a sustained pace.
Humans can sprint faster over very short distances than many other mammals can.
Sweating causes humans to lose significant amounts of water and salt during prolonged exercise.
A few mammals, such as horses, are also able to cool themselves by sweating.

questions.passage: Noticing that neighborhoods with more street trees tended to have lower crime rates, a city official concluded that planting more trees would reduce crime.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the official's conclusion?
options: Street trees provide shade that makes sidewalks more pleasant to walk along in summer.
A few neighborhoods with high crime rates have very few street trees.
Newly planted street trees can take many years to grow to their full height.
Wealthier neighborhoods tend both to have more street trees and to have lower crime, for reasons unrelated to the trees themselves.

questions.passage: A linguist claimed that a certain endangered language is being abandoned not because its speakers are forbidden to use it but because speaking it offers them no economic advantage.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the linguist's claim?
options: The language possesses a rich oral literature that has never been written down.
In surveys, parents who spoke the language reported choosing not to teach it to their children because the jobs available in the region required fluency in the national language instead.
No government has ever passed a law restricting the use of the language.
The language is spoken today by fewer than a thousand people.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • The Rosetta Stone is an ancient stone slab discovered in Egypt in 1799.
  • It is inscribed with the same text in three scripts: hieroglyphic, Demotic, and ancient Greek.
  • At the time of its discovery, scholars could already read ancient Greek.
  • By comparing the Greek text with the hieroglyphs, scholars began to decipher Egyptian hieroglyphic writing.
  • The decipherment was largely completed by Jean-François Champollion in 1822.
questions.question: The student wants to explain how the Rosetta Stone made the decipherment of hieroglyphs possible. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: The Rosetta Stone, discovered in Egypt in 1799, is inscribed in three different scripts.
The decipherment of the hieroglyphs was largely completed by Jean-François Champollion in 1822.
The Rosetta Stone is inscribed in hieroglyphic, Demotic, and ancient Greek.
Because the Rosetta Stone repeats the same text in ancient Greek—which scholars could already read—alongside the hieroglyphs, it allowed scholars to begin deciphering hieroglyphic writing.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Many species of bats hunt in complete darkness.
  • They emit high-pitched sounds and then listen for the returning echoes.
  • The time an echo takes to return indicates how far away an object is.
  • A change in the echo's pitch can indicate whether prey is moving toward or away from the bat.
  • This whole system is called echolocation.
questions.question: The student wants to explain how echolocation lets a bat locate and track moving prey in the dark. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Many species of bats are able to hunt in complete darkness.
The system bats use to navigate and hunt in the dark is called echolocation.
Through echolocation, a bat emits sounds and reads the returning echoes—using their timing to judge an object's distance and their shifting pitch to tell whether prey is approaching or retreating.
Bats emit high-pitched sounds and then listen for the echoes that return to them.

questions.passage: For decades, the vast stretches of the human genome that do not code for proteins were dismissed as "junk"—evolutionary debris of no particular function. That verdict is now being revised. Much of this noncoding DNA, researchers find, regulates when and how the coding genes switch on and off, orchestrating the delicate timing on which an organism's development depends. To have called it junk, it turns out, said less about the DNA itself than about the limits of what its first investigators knew how to look for.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The overwhelming majority of the human genome codes directly for proteins.
Researchers have now confirmed that noncoding DNA is indeed functionless evolutionary debris.
Noncoding DNA, once dismissed as useless 'junk,' is now understood to perform important regulatory functions that earlier researchers failed to recognize.
The timing of an organism's development depends entirely on its protein-coding genes.

questions.passage: The phrase "the fall of Rome" conjures a single catastrophe: barbarians at the gates, an entire civilization extinguished overnight. Yet across much of the former empire the transition was so gradual as to be nearly imperceptible to those living through it. Roman law, language, and administration persisted for generations under new rulers who often thought of themselves not as destroying Rome but as continuing it. What looks, from the distance of centuries, like a sudden fall may have felt, up close, more like a slow change of management.
questions.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The fall of Rome was a single catastrophe that extinguished the civilization almost overnight.
The rulers who succeeded Rome set out deliberately to destroy its law, language, and administration.
People living through the fall of Rome were acutely aware that their civilization was coming to an end.
What is remembered as Rome's sudden fall was, in many regions, a gradual transition in which Roman institutions persisted under new rulers.

questions.passage: My grandfather distrusted anything that ran too smoothly. A watch that never needed adjusting, he said, was a watch that had quietly stopped telling you anything true; it was the small daily corrections—the winding, the setting, the patient coaxing back into time—that kept a man honest about how far the world is always drifting. He spoke of clocks, but I understood, even as a boy, that he was not speaking only of clocks.
questions.question: The narrator suggests that his grandfather's remarks about clocks were also meant to convey a broader lesson about
options: the clear superiority of old craftsmanship over modern manufacturing
the value of steady attention and small, continual corrections in a life
the impossibility of ever measuring the passage of time accurately
the importance of choosing a steady and trustworthy profession

questions.passage: The ecologist Dara Whitfield hypothesized that a certain fish species keeps a coral reef healthy by eating the algae that would otherwise smother the coral; remove the fish, she predicted, and the algae would quickly overrun the reef.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Whitfield's hypothesis?
options: The fish species is brightly colored and is popular with recreational divers.
Coral reefs support a greater diversity of species than almost any other marine habitat.
On reef sections where the fish were experimentally excluded by nets, algae grew thick and coral cover declined, while adjacent open sections remained healthy.
The fish occasionally eat tiny amounts of coral along with the algae.

questions.passage: A study reported that students who used a new tutoring app scored higher on a standardized math test than students who did not, and the study's authors concluded that the app improves students' math skills.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the authors' conclusion?
options: The app was available only to students whose families paid for a premium subscription—students who also tended to attend better-funded schools.
The math test covered some material that the app did not directly address.
A few students reported finding the app's interface difficult to use at first.
Students who used the app tended to do so late in the evening.

questions.passage: A historian argued that a certain medieval town's sudden prosperity in the 1200s resulted chiefly from its acquiring the right to hold a weekly market, which drew traders from across the surrounding countryside.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the historian's argument?
options: The town lay beside a river that had been used for transport since well before the 1200s.
Town records show that the number of resident merchants and the total value of goods traded both rose sharply in the years immediately after the market charter was granted.
Several nearby towns were also granted the right to hold markets during the same century.
The town's population had already been growing slowly for a hundred years before the charter.

questions.passage: A scholar contends that beneath the cheerful surface of a certain poet's nursery rhymes runs a pointed critique of the social order of his day.
questions.question: Which quotation from the rhymes would best support the scholar's contention?
options: The lambs are in the meadow, the birds are in the tree, / and all the world is merry as a summer world can be.
Come, children, clap your hands and sing, / for spring has turned the barren fields to green.
The moon is a silver sixpence tossed up into the night's dark purse.
The rich man in his carriage rides warm above the mud / that the poor man, trudging homeward, carries on his boots and blood.

questions.passage: A geologist proposed that a thin layer of unusual sediment found at the same depth all over the world was deposited by the impact of a large asteroid rather than by ordinary erosion.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the geologist's proposal?
options: The sediment layer is measurably thicker in some regions of the world than in others.
Ordinary erosion is well known to deposit layers of sediment over very long periods.
The sediment layer contains high concentrations of iridium, an element rare in Earth's crust but abundant in asteroids.
The sediment layer everywhere lies directly above older layers of ordinary rock.

questions.passage: A newspaper columnist observed that countries whose populations drink more milk tend to produce more Nobel laureates, and suggested that drinking milk fosters the kind of thinking that wins Nobel Prizes.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken the columnist's suggestion?
options: Milk is a good dietary source of calcium and vitamin D.
Countries that consume more milk also tend to be considerably wealthier, with far greater resources to devote to scientific research and higher education.
A number of Nobel laureates have said that they rarely drink milk.
Nobel Prizes have been awarded every year since the early twentieth century.

questions.passage: An economist argued that a city's new bike-share program reduced automobile traffic not merely by replacing some car trips with bike trips but by prompting former drivers to give up owning cars altogether.
questions.question: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the economist's argument?
options: The bike-share bicycles were used most heavily during the morning and evening rush hours.
In the two years after the program launched, the number of car-free households in the city rose sharply, while it held steady in comparable cities that had no such program.
In surveys, many residents said they found the bike-share bicycles pleasant and convenient to use.
The city happened to open several new bike lanes in the same month that the program launched.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Mary Shelley (1797–1851) was an English writer.
  • She began writing Frankenstein when she was only eighteen years old.
  • The novel was first published anonymously in 1818.
  • It is often described as one of the earliest works of science fiction.
  • Its full title is Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus.
questions.question: The student wants to emphasize Frankenstein's significance in the history of science fiction. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Frankenstein, published anonymously in 1818, is often described as one of the earliest works of science fiction.
Mary Shelley, who lived from 1797 to 1851, was an English writer.
Mary Shelley began writing Frankenstein when she was only eighteen years old.
The full title of the novel is Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • Smallpox was a deadly contagious disease that killed hundreds of millions of people over the centuries.
  • A vaccine against smallpox was developed by Edward Jenner in 1796.
  • A coordinated global vaccination campaign was carried out during the twentieth century.
  • The last known natural case of smallpox occurred in 1977.
  • In 1980, the World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated.
questions.question: The student wants to explain how smallpox became the first human disease to be eradicated. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Smallpox was a deadly contagious disease that killed hundreds of millions of people over the centuries.
Edward Jenner developed the first vaccine against smallpox in 1796.
Following a coordinated global vaccination campaign, smallpox saw its last known natural case in 1977 and was declared eradicated by the World Health Organization in 1980.
In 1980, the World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated.
